source_triage.description_long: A March 2026 Chronicle essay by former NIH program official Elizabeth Ginexi analyzed funding-opportunity notices listed on Grants.gov. She reported that NIH posted 756 notices in 2024, 120 in 2025, and 14 by March 15, 2026. Ginexi also counted 75 NIH notices forecast for 2026, of which 61 had not yet been published. These numbers concern Notices of Funding Opportunities, which announce research areas and invite applications; they are not counts of grants awarded or dollars disbursed. A May 2026 VPM report republished NPR reporting on delays in NIH funding and included the administration’s explanation that a shutdown and congressional Democrats contributed to delays. The sources document a sharp reduction in posted opportunities and a slowdown researchers experienced. They do not establish that the agency acted covertly, that it shifted to larger awards to inflate totals, or that a particular budget was secretly withheld. Ginexi’s figures are an attributed analysis rather than an official NIH finding, so a correction should name the metric, date, and source.

frozen_original.title: FEC Paralyzed: Trump Fires Democratic Commissioner, Leaves Agency Without Quorum for 80% of Second Term
frozen_original.synopsis: In early 2025, Trump fired FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub — a Democrat who had served since 2002, well past her term — in a move she and most legal experts called illegal and unprecedented; two Republican commissioners also departed, leaving the agency below the four-commissioner quorum required to conduct any substantive business. On May 1, 2025, the FEC formally entered a de facto shutdown: it could no longer investigate complaints, levy fines, issue rules, offer formal legal guidance, or hold public meetings. Trump then declined for more than nine months to nominate replacements, leaving the FEC idled as the 2026 midterm election cycle got underway. By March 2026, the agency reported 195 pending enforcement matters with no action possible; its fine assessment for fiscal year 2026 stood at zero dollars. Trump finally nominated two Republicans in February 2026, but as of mid-2026 the Senate had not scheduled confirmation hearings. Weintraub told NPR: There's no cop on the beat. We will see billions of dollars raised and spent in the upcoming elections and at the moment there is no cop on the beat to make sure it's all being done in a lawful and transparent way. A NOTUS analysis found the FEC had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term.

staged_description.description_short: FEC operates without a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term

After additional commissioner departures, the FEC fell below its four-member voting threshold on May 1, 2025. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that the agency had 195 pending enforcement matters and later calculated that it had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump's second term. The prolonged lack of quorum prevented substantive enforcement votes.
staged_description.description_long: President Donald Trump sent Federal Election Commission Commissioner Ellen Weintraub a letter on Jan. 31, 2025, purporting to remove her. Weintraub disputed the move’s legality. After additional commissioner departures, the six-member FEC fell below the four members required for a quorum on May 1. Without a quorum, the commission could not take substantive enforcement votes, leaving complaints and investigations pending while it lacked enough members to act. NOTUS reported in March 2026 that 195 enforcement matters were pending and later calculated that the FEC had lacked a quorum for nearly 80% of Trump’s second term. Those figures show the size of the backlog and the duration of the agency’s limited voting capacity; they do not establish that the backlog resulted entirely from Weintraub’s removal or that every pending matter concerned the president. The FEC announced Commissioner Allen Dickerson’s departure on April 30, just before the commission fell below its voting threshold. The episode combined a disputed removal with later vacancies that left the campaign-finance regulator unable to make certain enforcement decisions.

frozen_original.title: Trump Fires All NLRB and EEOC Board Members, Paralyzing Labor and Anti-Discrimination Enforcement
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump fired all sitting members of the National Labor Relations Board and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, reducing both bodies below the quorum necessary to take official actions, effectively paralyzing federal labor law enforcement and anti-discrimination enforcement for millions of American workers. The NLRB was left unable to prosecute unfair labor practice charges or certify union elections. The EEOC lost the ability to pursue systemic discrimination cases on behalf of workers facing discrimination based on race, gender, age, and disability. Legal scholars debated whether the firings were lawful given the statutory protections for these independent agency board members, with courts reaching conflicting conclusions. Labor unions and civil rights organizations called the actions an unprecedented attack on worker protections.

staged_description.description_short: Trump Removes NLRB Member and Two EEOC Commissioners, Leaving Both Bodies Without Quorums
staged_description.description_medium: On January 27, 2025, President Trump removed NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and fired two Democratic EEOC commissioners, Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. The removals left both independent bodies without the quorum required for some commission- or board-level decisions. The NLRB's regional enforcement work continued, but the Board could not issue decisions without a quorum.
staged_description.description_long: On January 27, 2025, President Donald Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and fired Equal Employment Opportunity Commission commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels. The dismissals left both independent bodies below the quorum needed for some board- or commission-level decisions. The NLRB could not issue Board decisions without a quorum, although its regional offices continued enforcement work; the EEOC likewise retained other members and agency functions. The two agencies oversee different areas of workplace rights: the NLRB handles labor relations and unfair labor practice matters, while the EEOC addresses employment discrimination. Losing a quorum therefore constrained particular collective actions rather than stopping every investigation or enforcement process. The removals also prompted legal challenges over the president’s authority to dismiss officials serving on independent agencies. The event was narrower than claims that Trump fired every member or paralyzed both organizations. Its immediate institutional effect was to limit formal action by the boards while leaving regional and other agency work in operation.

frozen_original.title: DOGE Team Accesses IRS Tax Records of Political Opponents
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, reports emerged that operatives working for Elon Musk's DOGE initiative had obtained access to IRS tax return databases and were reviewing the confidential tax records of political opponents, Democratic donors, and journalists. Federal law strictly prohibits unauthorized disclosure or use of individual tax returns, with criminal penalties. IRS career officials reportedly raised alarms internally but were overruled or sidelined by political appointees. Congressional Democrats demanded investigations and noted that using tax records to target political opponents echoed the abuses of the Nixon administration. The breach represented one of the most serious abuses of government data for political purposes in American history.

staged_description.description_short: DOGE Seeks Broad IRS Data Access; Treasury Agrees to Limit Access to Anonymized Data
staged_description.description_medium: DOGE personnel sought access to sensitive IRS systems as part of the administration's government-wide review. Treasury and White House officials subsequently agreed that the DOGE representative at IRS would have read-only access to anonymized tax data rather than individual taxpayer records. staged_description.description_long: In February 2025, DOGE personnel sought access to sensitive Internal Revenue Service systems during the administration’s government-wide review. The Washington Post reported both the initial request and a subsequent agreement by Treasury and White House officials to limit the DOGE representative’s access to read-only, anonymized tax data rather than individual taxpayer returns. The sequence matters: the request raised legitimate concerns because IRS records contain highly sensitive personal and financial information, but the reported access arrangement is not evidence that DOGE inspected identifiable returns. The materials supplied for this entry specifically do not substantiate claims that political opponents, donors or journalists were targeted. The issue is therefore the scope of requested access, the safeguards negotiated around it and the importance of protecting taxpayer confidentiality—not a demonstrated search of particular people’s files. Any later account of actual use would require separate reporting or records showing what data were available, what queries were made and whether the anonymization controls worked as described. Keeping those distinctions clear preserves the public-interest question about oversight of government data while avoiding an unsupported allegation of political surveillance through individual tax records.

frozen_original.title: Trump Claims to Know More About Solar Energy Than Anyone
frozen_original.synopsis: Trump asserted he knew more about solar energy than anyone, despite repeatedly getting basic facts about solar technology wrong in public statements. Trump had previously claimed solar panels were 'extremely expensive' and wouldn't work on cloudy days, claims contradicted by widely available data showing the dramatic decline in solar costs and the effectiveness of modern panels in varied conditions. staged_description.description_short: Trump Says He Knows More About Renewables Than 'Any Human Being on Earth'

He then said he loved solar but criticized what he described as a roughly 30-year payback period and limited power. The record should use the verified renewables quote and 2016 date rather than recasting it as a 2020 claim of unmatched solar expertise.
staged_description.description_long: On April 13, 2016, while campaigning for the Republican presidential nomination, Donald Trump appeared on Fox News’ Hannity program in Pittsburgh and discussed energy policy. He said he knew more about renewables than “any human being on earth,” then added that he loved solar while criticizing its payback period and power output. In the transcript, he described a 30-year payback and referred to a 32-year estimate raised in the discussion. The exchange also included his argument that the United States should use a range of energy sources, including renewables, while expanding coal production. The quote is a verifiable campaign-era boast, but the transcript alone does not establish Trump’s comparative expertise or resolve the technical merits of his payback claims; those depend on system costs, financing, location and assumptions that were not examined in the exchange. The record’s correction is important because it places the remark in 2016 and describes it as a claim about renewables generally, not a 2020 assertion limited to solar. It captures his rhetoric and stated position, not an expert assessment of renewable economics.

staged_description.description_long:
Stephen Miller, serving as White House deputy chief of staff, played a central role in shaping and driving the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration agenda. A Reuters profile published July 11, 2025, described him as the White House aide driving that agenda and reported on his policy influence. The record concerns his central role in the administration’s direction, rather than claiming that he alone created every part of its immigration program.

That distinction matters because a broad policy agenda involves executive actions, legal arguments, and enforcement operations, and the available account does not establish that Miller personally drafted each order or designed every procedure. The supported description is that he was an influential architect and driver of the crackdown. It does not attribute every legal theory, operational decision, or government action to him without specific documentation.

The administration’s immigration agenda raised significant human-rights concerns, reflected in this entry’s category. The supplied source supports Miller’s central policy role, but does not, by itself, establish the consequences of any individual policy or quantify enforcement outcomes. This entry therefore focuses on his documented influence and avoids an unsupported claim that the administration had already conducted the largest deportation operation in American history.

frozen_original.title: Trump Ends Mental Health Parity Enforcement — Insurers Free to Discriminate
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration rescinded Biden-era enforcement regulations implementing the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, which required insurance plans to provide equivalent coverage for mental health and substance use disorder treatment as for physical health conditions. The rollback effectively freed insurers to reimpose prior authorization requirements, lower reimbursement rates, and narrower provider networks for mental health care. The decision came amid record demand for mental health services and a national opioid crisis that had already killed over a million Americans. Mental health advocates called it an abandonment of the 74 million Americans with mental illness who relied on parity protections. The American Psychiatric Association condemned the action as a step backward that would drive people out of care.

staged_description.description_short: Agencies Pause Enforcement of New 2024 Mental Health Parity Rule Provisions

The policy explicitly left MHPAEA's statutory obligations and the earlier 2013 rule in effect. The stored March date and claim that parity enforcement ended entirely are inaccurate.
staged_description.description_long:
On May 15, 2025, the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury announced that they would not enforce the new portions of the 2024 final rule implementing the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) while litigation and reconsideration continued. The departments’ statement, linked here, makes an important distinction: the pause concerned provisions added by the 2024 rule, not the entire legal framework for mental-health and substance-use-disorder coverage.

The agencies said that MHPAEA’s statutory obligations remained in effect, as did the earlier 2013 rule. The action therefore did not simply end parity enforcement or make insurers free of all parity requirements. It changed the enforcement status of new requirements in the 2024 rule during a period of legal challenge and reconsideration. That distinction corrects the original entry’s inaccurate March 2025 date and overbroad claim that enforcement had ended altogether. The announcement left existing obligations intact while creating uncertainty about when, or in what form, the newer provisions might be enforced. The supplied information does not specify the outcome of the litigation or subsequent reconsideration, so no further conclusion about the rule’s ultimate status is warranted here.

frozen_original.title: NLRB Rendered Non-Functional — Trump Fires All Board Members
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump fired all sitting members of the National Labor Relations Board — the independent federal agency responsible for enforcing workers' rights to organize, collectively bargain, and engage in protected concerted activity — leaving the board without a quorum and effectively unable to adjudicate any labor disputes. The firings were unprecedented; NLRB members serve fixed terms and had historically been removed only for cause. Without a quorum, hundreds of pending cases involving union elections, unfair labor practice charges, and worker retaliation complaints were frozen. The board's general counsel was also fired. Labor law experts described the action as the most significant attack on workers' right to organize in modern American history, leaving approximately 100 million private-sector workers without an enforcement body for their federal labor rights.

staged_description.title: Trump Fires NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo
staged_description.description_short: Trump Fires NLRB Member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo
staged_description.description_medium: Trump fired NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo in late January 2025. Because the five-member board already had two vacancies, Wilcox's removal deprived it of a quorum and temporarily prevented it from issuing decisions. The stored claim that Trump fired all board members on January 20 is false.
staged_description.description_long:
Trump removed National Labor Relations Board member Gwynne Wilcox and General Counsel Jennifer Abruzzo in late January 2025. Reuters reported the dismissals on January 28. Wilcox's departure affected the Board's ability to act: with two seats already vacant, the five-member body no longer had a quorum.

Without a quorum, the NLRB temporarily could not issue decisions. Abruzzo held a separate leadership position, so her dismissal did not count as another removal from the five-member Board. The distinction explains why Wilcox's removal, specifically, changed the Board's decision-making capacity.

The dismissals marked a significant intervention in agency leadership, but they did not remove every sitting Board member, and the reported date was not January 20. Loss of a quorum also did not mean that every NLRB function disappeared. The immediate consequence was a temporary limit on Board decisions while the agency's membership and leadership changed. Later staffing or litigation developments are separate from these January removals.

staged_description.description_long: By April 2025, reporting based on court filings described Department of Government Efficiency personnel as having access to numerous Department of Health and Human Services systems, including financial, program, and some case-management databases. Separate reporting said DOGE received read-only access to a child-support database containing sensitive income information. These disclosures raised privacy and security concerns because access involved information held by federal health and service agencies. The available evidence in the supplied correction does not establish the original, stronger allegation that DOGE had unrestricted access to complete medical records for millions of Americans, including HIV status, mental-health diagnoses, and prescription histories. The distinction between access to multiple systems and unrestricted access to all detailed medical records is material. This entry documents the reported scope and the limits of what had been verified by April 2025; it does not establish that every DOGE employee saw every record or that data was misused. The titles and dates from the corrected entry are preserved. Any later expansion of access or finding of improper use should be supported by separate court filings, agency records, or reporting.
